subject: maths
title: Pie Charts and Line Graphs
seo_title: Year 6 Pie Charts and Line Graphs Worksheets: Fractions, Angles and Reading Scales (Free, with Answers)
standard_text: Interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs and use these to solve problems.
meta_desc: Free Year 6 maths worksheets on pie charts and line graphs: read sectors as fractions and percentages, work out angles out of 360°, read line graph scales and compare two pie charts. 100 SATs-style questions with an answer key, following the National Curriculum.
key_big: A pie chart shows fractions of a whole. The whole circle is 360°.
key_sub: Find the fraction, then the fraction of the total. Each person is 360 ÷ total degrees. On a line graph, check what each small square is worth, and look for the steepest part for the fastest change.
body_html:
A pie chart shows parts of a whole

A pie chart is a circle split into sectors. The whole circle is everyone in the survey. Each sector shows a fraction of the total, not a number of people.

Example 1

How many of the 40 pupils chose netball?

Netball is 2 of the 8 parts = 14. 14 of 40 = 40 ÷ 4 = 10.

Answer: 10 pupils

Angles in a pie chart

The angles at the centre add up to 360°. To draw a pie chart, find how many degrees each person is worth: 360 ÷ total.

SportPupilsAngle (9° each)
Football2020 × 9 = 180°
Netball1010 × 9 = 90°
Swimming55 × 9 = 45°
Cricket55 × 9 = 45°
Total40360°
Example 2

60 people were asked. 15 chose tennis. What angle is the tennis sector?

360 ÷ 60 = 6° for each person. 15 × 6 = 90°.

Answer: 90°

To go back from an angle to people, divide: a sector of 120° with 6° for each person is 120 ÷ 6 = 20 people.

Read a line graph

A line graph shows how something changes over time. First check the scale: what is each small square worth? Go up from the bottom axis to the line, then across to the scale. A steeper line means a faster change. A flat line means no change.

Example 3

How much did the temperature fall from 14:00 to 18:00?

14:00: 14 °C. 18:00: 8 °C. 14 − 8 = 6.

Answer: 6 °C

Comparing two pie charts

A bigger sector is a bigger fraction. It is only more people if both pie charts show the same total. Always work out the numbers: 13 of 24 = 8, but 14 of 60 = 15.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading a sector as a number of peopleFind the fraction, then the fraction of the total
Using 100 instead of 360 for anglesAngles add up to 360°; percentages add up to 100%
Saying a bigger sector always means more peopleCheck the totals of both pie charts
Counting each small square on a line graph as 1Work out the scale: labels 0, 10, 20 with 5 squares means 2 each
Choosing the highest point for the fastest changeFastest change is the steepest part of the line

faq.q: How do you work out the angles for a pie chart?
faq.a: Divide 360 by the total to find the angle for one item, then multiply by each amount. For 60 people, each person is 360 ÷ 60 = 6°, so 15 people get 15 × 6 = 90°.

faq.q: How do you read a pie chart in Year 6?
faq.a: Work out what fraction or percentage of the circle the sector is, then find that fraction of the total. If a quarter of 40 pupils chose swimming, 40 ÷ 4 = 10 pupils chose swimming.

faq.q: What is a line graph used for?
faq.a: A line graph shows how something changes over time, such as temperature, height or distance. A steeper line shows a faster change, and a flat line shows no change.

faq.q: Are pie charts and line graphs in the Year 6 SATs?
faq.a: Yes, statistics questions can appear in the KS2 SATs reasoning papers. Pupils may be asked to read values, find fractions or angles of a pie chart, or compare and calculate from a line graph.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils chose football?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Football has 4 of them: 48 = 12.

items.q: Which sport was chosen by a quarter of the pupils?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Netball has 2 of them: 28 = 14.

items.q: Which colour was chosen by a quarter of the pupils?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Blue has 2 of them: 28 = 14.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils chose red?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Red has 3 of them: 38.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils walk to school?
items.e: The circle is split into 6 equal parts. Walk has 3 of them: 36 = 12.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils come by car?
items.e: The circle is split into 6 equal parts. Car has 2 of them: 26 = 13.

items.q: Which ways of travelling make half of the pie chart together?
items.e: Half of 6 parts is 3 parts. Car has 2 parts and Bus has 1 part: 2 + 1 = 3, so Car and Bus make 36 = 12.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils have a cat?
items.e: The circle is split into 12 equal parts. Cat has 3 of them: 312 = 14.

items.q: Which pet is 16 of the pie chart?
items.e: The circle is split into 12 equal parts. Fish has 2 of them: 212 = 16.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils did not choose blue?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Blue has 2 of them, so 8 − 2 = 6 parts are not Blue: 68 = 34.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils chose an apple or a pear?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Apple and Pear have 2 of them: 28 = 14.

items.q: Which fruit was chosen by half of the pupils?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Grapes has 4 of them: 48 = 12.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils chose pasta?
items.e: The circle is split into 10 equal parts. Pasta has 4 of them: 410 = 25.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils have a dog or a cat?
items.e: The circle is split into 12 equal parts. Dog and Cat have 9 of them: 912 = 34.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils chose curry or pizza?
items.e: The circle is split into 10 equal parts. Curry and Pizza have 5 of them: 510 = 12.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils chose spring?
items.e: The circle is split into 12 equal parts. Spring has 3 of them: 312 = 14.

items.q: Which season was chosen by 512 of the pupils?
items.e: The circle is split into 12 equal parts. Summer has 5 of them: 512.

items.q: Which subject was chosen by 38 of the pupils?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Science has 3 of them: 38.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils chose maths or art?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Maths and Art have 4 of them: 48 = 12.

items.q: What fraction of the pupils did not choose science?
items.e: The circle is split into 8 equal parts. Science has 3 of them, so 8 − 3 = 5 parts are not Science: 58.

sets.title: Pie charts: find amounts and percentages

items.q: How many pupils come by car?
items.e: Car is 2 of the 8 equal parts: 28 = 14 of the pie. 14 of 40 = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 pupils.

items.q: How many pupils walk to school?
items.e: Walk is half of the pie. Half of 40 = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 pupils.

items.q: How many pupils cycle to school?
items.e: Bike is 1 of the 8 equal parts: 18 of 40 = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 pupils.

items.q: 200 pupils chose their favourite ice lolly. How many chose orange?
items.e: 10% of 200 = 200 ÷ 10 = 20. So 30% = 3 × 20 = 60 pupils. (30% is not 30 pupils: there are 200 pupils, not 100.)

items.q: 200 pupils chose their favourite ice lolly. How many more chose lemon than cherry?
What percentage of the families went to France?
items.e: The circle is split into 10 equal parts, so each part is 10%. France has 3 parts: 3 × 10% = 30%.

items.q: How many of the 50 families went to Spain?
items.e: Spain has 4 of the 10 parts: 410 = 40%. 10% of 50 = 5, so 40% = 4 × 5 = 20 families.

items.q: How many pupils chose apples?
items.e: Apple is 2 of the 6 equal parts: 26 = 13. 13 of 60 = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 pupils.

items.q: 12 pupils chose swimming. How many pupils were asked altogether?
items.e: Swimming is 2 of the 8 parts = 14 of the pie. If 14 is 12 pupils, the whole is 4 × 12 = 48 pupils.

items.q: 9 pupils chose rugby. How many pupils were asked altogether?
items.e: 10% is 9 pupils. 100% is 10 times as many: 10 × 9 = 90 pupils.

items.q: How many adults chose tea?
items.e: 25% = 14. 14 of 300 = 300 ÷ 4 = 75 adults.

items.q: How many pupils have a packed lunch?
items.e: Packed lunch is 3 of the 8 equal parts: 38. 64 ÷ 8 = 8, so 38 = 3 × 8 = 24 pupils.

items.q: How many pupils go home for lunch?
items.e: Home is 1 of the 8 equal parts: 18 of 64 = 64 ÷ 8 = 8 pupils.

items.q: How many pupils chose juice?
How many pupils chose milk?
How many of the cars are silver?
items.e: Each of the 10 equal parts is 10%. Silver has 4 parts = 40%. 40% of 100 = 40 cars.

items.q: What percentage of the cars are not black?
items.e: Black is 3 of the 10 parts = 30%. Not black: 100% − 30% = 70%.

items.q: How many pupils chose swimming?
items.e: The circle has 12 equal parts. Swimming has 2: 212 = 16. 120 ÷ 6 = 20 pupils.

items.q: How many pupils in 6B chose maths?
24 pupils chose their favourite lesson. 6 pupils chose art. What fraction of the pie chart is art?
items.e: Art is 6 out of all 24 pupils (not out of the other 18): 624. Divide both numbers by 6: 14.

items.q: All the angles in a pie chart add up to …
items.e: A pie chart is a whole circle, and the angles at the centre of a circle add up to 360°. (100 is for percentages.)

items.q: A pie chart shows 20 pupils. How many degrees stand for each pupil?
items.e: The whole circle is 360°. 360 ÷ 20 = 18°, so each pupil is 18°. (100 ÷ 20 = 5 uses 100, not 360.)

items.q: A pie chart shows 60 people. How many degrees stand for each person?
items.e: 360 ÷ 60 = 6, so each person is 6°.

items.q: 60 people were asked. 15 chose swimming. What angle should the swimming sector be?
items.e: Each person is 360 ÷ 60 = 6°. 15 × 6 = 90°. (Or: 15 out of 60 is 14, and 14 of 360° = 90°.)

items.q: 24 pupils were asked. 8 chose cricket. What angle should the cricket sector be?
items.e: Each pupil is 360 ÷ 24 = 15°. 8 × 15 = 120°. (Or: 8 out of 24 is 13, and 13 of 360° = 120°.)

items.q: 30 pupils were asked. 9 chose art. What angle should the art sector be?
A sector of a pie chart has an angle of 90°. What fraction of the pie chart is it?
items.e: Compare with the whole circle: 90360 = 14. (90100 uses 100, not 360.)

items.q: A sector of a pie chart has an angle of 120°. What fraction of the pie chart is it?
items.e: 120360 = 13. Three sectors of 120° make 360°.

items.q: A sector of a pie chart has an angle of 45°. What percentage of the pie chart is it?
items.e: 45360 = 18. 18 = 100% ÷ 8 = 12.5%.

items.q: A sector is 16 of a pie chart. What is its angle?
A sector is 25% of a pie chart. What is its angle?
items.e: 25% = 14. 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

items.q: What is the angle of the Other sector?
What is the angle of the Swimming sector?
How many pupils chose football?
items.e: Each pupil is 360 ÷ 36 = 10°. 150 ÷ 10 = 15 pupils.

items.q: 45 pupils were asked. 18 chose football. What angle should the football sector be?
In a pie chart each pupil is 12°. The netball sector is 84°. How many pupils chose netball?
In a pie chart, a sector of 72° stands for 10 people. How many people does the whole pie chart show?
items.e: 72° × 5 = 360°, so the whole pie chart is 5 times as big as the sector: 5 × 10 = 50 people.

items.q: How many more pupils walk than come by car?
40 pupils were asked about pets: cat 10, dog 14, fish 6, other 10. What angle should the dog sector be?
How many pupils walk?
items.e: Each pupil is 360 ÷ 18 = 20°. 140 ÷ 20 = 7 pupils.

items.q: What was the temperature at 10:00?
items.e: Go up from 10:00 to the point, then across. Each small square is 1 °C. The point is 2 squares above 0, so 2 °C.

items.q: What was the lowest temperature?
items.e: The lowest point is at 06:00. It is 3 squares below 0, so −3 °C.

items.q: How much warmer was it at 14:00 than at 06:00?
items.e: 14:00: 6 °C. 06:00: −3 °C. From −3 up to 0 is 3, and from 0 up to 6 is 6: 3 + 6 = 9 °C.

items.q: Between which two times did the temperature rise the most?
items.e: Look for the steepest part going up. From 08:00 to 10:00 it rose from −2 °C to 2 °C: 4 °C. From 10:00 to 12:00 it rose only 3 °C.

items.q: At what time was the temperature 5 °C?
items.e: Find 5 on the scale and go across to the line. The point at 5 °C is above 12:00.

items.q: How tall was the bean plant in week 3?
items.e: The numbers go up in 10s, but each small square is 2 cm. Week 3 is 2 squares above 10: 10 + 2 + 2 = 14 cm. (7 counts the squares as 1 cm each.)

items.q: How much did the plant grow from week 2 to week 5?
items.e: Week 2: 8 cm. Week 5: 22 cm. 22 − 8 = 14 cm. (22 cm is the height, not the growth.)

items.q: Between which two weeks did the plant grow the most?
items.e: The steepest part of the line is from week 2 (8 cm) to week 3 (14 cm): 6 cm. The highest point (week 6) is the tallest, not the fastest growth.

items.q: In which week did the plant first reach 18 cm?
items.e: Find 18 cm on the scale (4 small squares above 10) and go across to the line, then down: week 4.

items.q: How far had Kai cycled by 10:20?
items.e: Go up from 10:20 to the point. It is on the line for 20, so 20 km.

items.q: Kai stopped for a rest. When was he resting?
items.e: When Kai stops, the distance does not change, so the line is flat. From 09:40 to 10:00 it stays at 12 km.

items.q: When was Kai cycling fastest?
items.e: Fastest means the most distance in the same time: the steepest part. From 10:00 to 10:20 he went 20 − 12 = 8 km. In every other 20 minutes he went 6 km or less.

items.q: How far did Kai cycle between 09:20 and 10:40?
How much warmer was London than Edinburgh in April?
items.e: April: London 12 °C, Edinburgh 8 °C. 12 − 8 = 4 °C.

items.q: In which month was the temperature the same in both cities?
items.e: The two lines meet at January: both are 4 °C.

items.q: By how much did Edinburgh’s temperature rise from February to June?
items.e: Use the dashed line (Edinburgh). February: 4 °C. June: 14 °C. 14 − 4 = 10 °C. (12 °C uses the London line.)

items.q: What was the temperature of the water after 10 minutes?
items.e: The labels go up in 20s, so each square is 10 °C. At 10 minutes the point is halfway between 60 and 70: 65 °C.

items.q: How much did the water cool in the first 5 minutes?
items.e: 0 minutes: 100 °C. 5 minutes: 80 °C. 100 − 80 = 20 °C. After that it cools more slowly.

items.q: Use the graph to change 25 miles into kilometres.
items.e: 25 miles is halfway between 20 and 30. Go up to the line and across: 40 km. (The labels go up in 16s and each square is 8 km.)

items.q: Use the graph to change 64 km into miles.
items.e: Find 64 on the kilometres scale, go across to the line, then down: 40 miles.

sets.title: Compare pie charts and solve problems

items.q: Which class has more pupils who chose football?
items.e: 6A: 23 of 24 = 16 pupils. 6B: 13 of 60 = 20 pupils. 6B has more, even though its sector is smaller, because 6B has more pupils.

items.q: How many more pupils chose netball in 6B than in 6A?
items.e: 6A netball: 16 of 24 = 4. 6B netball: 13 of 60 = 20. 20 − 4 = 16 pupils.

items.q: Mohammed says, “More pupils walk at School A, because its Walk sector is bigger.” Is he right?
items.e: School A: 14 of 120 = 30. School B: 16 of 300 = 50. The sector size only shows the fraction, not the number of pupils.

items.q: Ruby spent £32. How much did she spend on books?
items.e: £32 ÷ 8 = £4 for each of the 8 parts. Books has 3 parts: 3 × £4 = £12.

items.q: How much did Ruby spend on books and sweets together?
items.e: Books and sweets have 3 + 1 = 4 of the 8 parts: half of £32 = £16.

items.q: Which graph is best to show how the temperature changes during a day?
items.e: Temperature changes over time. A line graph joins the readings so you can see it rise and fall.

items.q: Which graph is best to show what fraction of a class chose each school dinner?
items.e: A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts, so you can see each fraction.

items.q: Which sentence about a pie chart is true?
c: A bigger sector always means more people
items.e: A pie chart is a circle, so the angles add up to 360°. A bigger sector is a bigger fraction, but only more people if the totals are the same.

items.q: In which month did the café first sell more ice creams than hot chocolates?
items.e: In March hot chocolate was 90 and ice cream 60, so hot chocolate was still more. In April ice cream was 80 and hot chocolate 60, so April is the first month.

items.q: How many more ice creams than hot chocolates were sold in June?
items.e: Each square is 20. June: ice cream 140, hot chocolate 20. 140 − 20 = 120.

items.q: How many visitors chose giraffes?
items.e: 360 visitors and 360°, so each visitor is 1°. The giraffes sector is 60°, so 60 visitors.

items.q: 30 pupils walk. How many pupils are in the survey altogether?
items.e: Walk is 120°, which is 13 of 360°. If 13 is 30 pupils, the whole is 3 × 30 = 90 pupils.

items.q: 7 pupils have no pets. How many pupils are in Isla’s class?
items.e: 25% = 14. If 14 is 7 pupils, the whole class is 4 × 7 = 28 pupils.

items.q: Which year group has more pupils who chose art?
items.e: Year 5: 25% of 80 = 20 pupils. Year 6: 30% of 60 = 18 pupils. Year 6 has the bigger percentage, but Year 5 has more pupils.

items.q: How many pupils chose PE altogether in Year 5 and Year 6?
items.e: Year 5: 50% of 80 = 40. Year 6: 40% of 60 = 24. 40 + 24 = 64 pupils. (90 adds the percentages.)

items.q: After week 6, the plant keeps growing at the same rate as from week 5 to week 6. How tall will it be in week 8?
items.e: Week 5: 22 cm. Week 6: 24 cm. It grows 2 cm a week. Week 7: 26 cm. Week 8: 28 cm.

items.q: 1,200 people voted. In the pie chart, the Yes sector is 38 of the circle. How many people voted Yes?
items.e: 1,200 ÷ 8 = 150, so 18 is 150 people. 38 = 3 × 150 = 450 people.

items.q: Pie chart A shows 40 pupils and pie chart B shows 100 pupils. Both have a Walk sector of 90°. How many more pupils walk in B than in A?
items.e: 90° is 14 of a pie chart. A: 14 of 40 = 10. B: 14 of 100 = 25. 25 − 10 = 15 pupils. The same angle does not mean the same number.

items.q: Grace changes £35 into euros before her holiday. How many euros does she get?
items.e: £35 is halfway between £30 and £40. Go up to the line and across: halfway between €36 and €48 is €42. (Each square is €6.)

items.q: How many more hours does Harry spend sleeping than at school?
items.e: 24 hours = 360°, so 1 hour = 360 ÷ 24 = 15°. Sleep: 150 ÷ 15 = 10 hours. School: 90 ÷ 15 = 6 hours. 10 − 6 = 4 hours.
